title: Status page: soft-fail cascade — summary & customer actions (draft)
content:
PURPOSE
This is a customer-facing draft combining (A) a short statuspage message and (B) a more detailed post-incident summary customers can reference. The goal is concise clarity: what happened, who was affected, what we did, recommended customer actions, and next steps for prevention.

INTENDED AUDIENCE
- Technical product owners integrating Redwood inference APIs
- Platform/security contacts at customer orgs
- Partner SREs and integrators

SHORT STATUSPAGE TEXT (<= 400 chars) — suggested
Title: Partial request failures and elevated token latency (regional, intermittent)
Body: We experienced an issue affecting a subset of inference requests in US-west and EU-west where some calls returned partial outputs or experienced high token latency. We deployed a staged rollback to a stable routing policy at 2029-12-19 22:10 UTC and traffic has returned to baseline. We continue validation checks; no data loss detected.

SEAMLESS STATUSPAGE BULLETS (for the timeline block)
- Detection: 2029-12-19 20:47 UTC — automated anomaly detectors flagged a rise in partial responses and increased per-token latency.
- Scope triage: 20:48–21:05 UTC — SRE and Serving runtime identified elevated error rates concentrated on requests routed to a new multi-cluster routing policy (canary).
- Mitigation: 21:06–22:10 UTC — traffic rebalanced to stable routing (fallback), canary disabled, manual KV-cache warmup triggered for affected model variants.
- Recovery: 22:11 UTC — error rate and token latency back within SLOs for >95% of tenants.
- Monitoring: 22:11–ongoing — verification and increased sampling across tenant routes for four hours.

CUSTOMER-FACING POST-INCIDENT SUMMARY (long-form)
Executive summary
On 2029-12-19 between ~20:45–22:10 UTC we saw a regression in a recently deployed model routing optimization. The regression caused a soft-fail cascade: some requests routed to the canary path returned truncated outputs (partial tokens) or experienced prolonged per-token latency spikes due to an unexpected interaction between our continuous batching heuristics and a KV cache warmup sequence. The root cause was an ordering bug in the canary routing policy that allowed a small percentage of short-lived worker processes to receive traffic before their KV cache primed. Those workers returned early partial responses or experienced token stalls.

Impact
- Affected customers: approx. 2.6% of active tenants routed through the canary region, primarily calling generation endpoints with short prompt prefixes and streaming enabled.
- Observable symptoms for customers: truncated/partial responses (stream closed early), higher-than-normal per-token latency, occasional 5xx codes for retries.
- Data integrity: no customer data was lost or exposed. Request bodies were processed only on ephemeral inference workers and log collection remains intact.

Immediate remediation actions taken
- Automated rollback of the canary routing policy at 21:06 UTC; manual rollback completed by 22:10 UTC.
- Forced KV-cache prewarm for affected worker pools and added a temporary conservative batching cap for short-sequence requests.
- Increased sampling in observability (trace-level sampling for five minutes per affected route) to validate response completeness.
- Notified customers via statuspage and direct tenant mailing list; Customer Success opened proactive outreach to tenants with signs of partial responses.

Customer actionable guidance (what you can do now)
- If you observed partial or truncated responses: re-run the affected requests; the platform should return full outputs now. For streaming clients, ensure your client is tolerant of intermittent early closures and employ an idempotent retry strategy.
- If you run high-throughput short-prefix workloads (e.g., prompt-to-completion < 16 tokens), consider temporarily toggling streaming=false for high-safety routes until we confirm final mitigations.
- If you see increased 5xx errors: implement client exponential backoff and report request IDs to support (provide request-id headers).

Timeline (detailed)
- 20:47 UTC — anomaly detectors triggered (partial response rate > baseline +6 sigma).
- 20:48–21:00 UTC — on-call SRE confirmed elevated partial-response metric; Serving-runtime leads joined.
- 21:00–21:06 UTC — root-cause hypothesis formed: ordering in routing policy + unprimed KV cache causing early flush.
- 21:06 UTC — disabled canary routing by policy and initiated traffic shift to stable pool.
- 21:20 UTC — first signs of recovery in token latency for major routes.
- 22:10 UTC — manual verification completed; traffic fully on stable policy, KV-cache warmed.
- 22:11 UTC — declared service stabilized; monitoring continues.

Root cause
A change in our multi-cluster routing logic allowed ephemeral worker instances to accept requests before KV cache priming completed when the worker lifecycle overlapped with continuous-batching windows. When such workers received streaming generation requests with short prompts, the runtime returned partial chunks and then closed the stream while background cache population continued. This manifested as a soft-fail cascade because downstream retries sometimes hit other unprimed workers.

Planned follow-up and prevention
- Short-term (next 48–72 hours): revert canary to conservative rollout thresholds, add mandatory KV prewarm at worker start for streaming and short-prefix paths, and extend canary sampling to include synthetic short-prefix traffic.
- Medium-term (2–6 weeks): add a routing invariant check in our deployment pipeline that blocks routing policy promotion if worker priming metrics are below threshold; add unit/integration tests covering worker start ordering relative to cache readiness.
- Long-term (3+ months): rework the startup lifecycle to make priming idempotent and observable in the control plane; formalize contract between routing policy and worker readiness so future optimizations cannot bypass priming.

Customer communication plan
- Immediate: statuspage update (this text trimmed) + tenant-targeted email with suggested actions.
- 24–72 hours: follow-up note summarizing verification checks and any additional mitigations.
- 2–6 weeks: formal customer-facing postmortem with root-cause artifacts and test plan.

Open items / internal questions (for PRD review)
- Do we need to provide per-tenant logs beyond request IDs to customers who reported partial outputs? Legal says only with customer consent; to discuss with CSMs.
- Should we default streaming=false on short-prefix requests for new customers until priming invariant is guaranteed? Product input needed.

DRAFT NOTES FOR EDITORS
- Tone: factual, brief, accountable. Avoid technical overload in the short status page blurb.
- Include a link to the incident postmortem (Confluence) and the status incident page.
- Prepare an inbox template for tenant replies; CS should escalate any reported data-loss immediately (we do not expect any).

SAMPLE TENANT EMAIL (short)
Subject: Redwood status: brief update on partial responses impacting a small subset of requests (Dec 19)
Body: Hi — we wanted to let you know about a transient issue that affected a small subset of inference requests on Dec 19. We reverted the routing change and verified service recovery; please re-run any requests that returned partial output and share request-ids with Support if you continue to see issues. Full summary and next steps are here: https://status.redwood.ai/incidents/2029-12-19-soft-fail-cascade.

SIGN-OFF
Prepared by: Marcos Rivera (Customer Success), with technical input from Serving Runtime and SRE.
Status: draft for review by eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, product-hosted-api, legal.

-- END --
